paper_title: Stable Gated DeltaNet-2: Understanding and Mitigating Recurrent State Instability

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Linear attention offers an efficient solution for long-sequence modeling via linear complexity and fixed-size recurrent states. Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) introduces independent channel-wise control over erasure and writing, enhancing state-update expressiveness and in-context retrieval, yet it suffers from training failures during long-context training. We trace these failures to the asymmetry between reading and modification directions during erasure, which yields non-normal erase operators whose directional gains accumulate across tokens, triggering exponential state growth even without new writes. To resolve this, we propose \model{}, employing symmetric erasure to ensure non-expansive state propagation and decay-regulated residual writing to preserve writing flexibility. Theoretically, we establish an $O(\sqrt{T})$ upper bound on recurrent state growth while retaining chunkwise parallel computation. Experiments on ~1.6B parameter models show that \model{} achieves stable training alongside improved long-context retrieval. Compared to GDN-2, it boosts the 128K average RULER score by 6.80 points in the recurrent setting and average accuracy across nine downstream tasks by 0.62 points in the hybrid setting.

Benjamin Franklin The growing demand for long-context understanding and extended generation (Sun et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026) has made efficient sequence modeling an increasingly important challenge for large language models. To address the computational and memory bottlenecks of standard softmax attention (Llama, 2023; Lu et al., 2026), linear attention (Katharopoulos et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2023) has emerged as an efficient alternative that compresses historical information into fixed-size recurrent state, thereby enabling linear-time sequence processing and constant memory during autoregressive decoding. Building on this approach, recent advances in gating mechanisms and delta-rule-based updates (Yang et al., 2024a; 2025; 2024b) have substantially enhanced the expressiveness of recurrent memory, enabling more fine-grained control over information retention and modification. Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) (Hatamizadeh et al., 2026) further advances this line of work by replacing the shared scalar update gate in Gated DeltaNet (GDN) (Yang et al., 2025) and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) (Team et al., 2025) with independent channel-wise erase and write gates, supporting more expressive recurrent state updates and improved in-context retrieval. Specifically, the erase gate reweights the key coordinates used to read content for erasure, while the modification is applied along the original key, allowing more flexible selection of content for erasure. However, we argue that the asymmetry between the reading and modification directions during erasure in GDN2 constitutes an inherent source of instability in its recurrent dynamics, potentially triggering catastrophic state explosion and ultimately causing training failures at long context. Our analysis shows that the asymmetric coupling between the erase gate and the key can introduce shear, preserving some state components while inducing additional 1 Stable GDN-2 components along other directions, as illustrated in Figure 1(a). The resulting non-normal erasure operator can amplify certain state directions despite all its eigenvalues having magnitude at most one. When amplified output directions of earlier transitions align with expanding input directions of subsequent transitions, these gains can accumulate across the sequence, allowing the recurrent state to continue growing to the point of numerical overflow, even after new writes cease. As Franklin famously remarked, small leak will sink great ship. To thoroughly investigate the underlying mechanisms of this instability, we examine recurrent state dynamics and their numerical and representational consequences in practical training. At context length of 64K, we observe numerical failures across both pretraining and post-training settings, affecting recurrent as well as hybrid GDN-2 architectures. More importantly, numerical failures represent only the most visible manifestation of broader issue: even in runs that complete training with finite losses, individual entries of the recurrent state can exceed 1036, indicating substantial internal state amplification. Replay analysis shows that amplification from asymmetric erasure can concentrate state energy in dominant direction and sharply reduce effective capacity before numerical failure, with little warning in the training loss. These observations highlight fundamental limitation of loss-based monitoring and motivate closer investigation of the underlying recurrent state dynamics that govern memory propagation over long sequences. These findings motivate Stable GDN-2, which controls recurrent state amplification through symmetric erasure while retaining channel-wise gating. Distributing the erase gate symmetrically across the two key factors aligns the reading and modification directions, ensuring non-expansive propagation under the standard key normalization and gate constraints, as illustrated in Figure 1(b). To complement the resulting gated write, we introduce residual writing path whose amplitude is regulated by decay. This design supports additional writing in channels where the erase gate is small while controlling the energy introduced by the residual. The update retains an input-dependent affine structure compatible with chunk-wise parallel computation. We evaluate Stable GDN-2 through 64K-context pretraining in recurrent and hybrid architectures, comparing language modeling, downstream performance, and longcontext retrieval against GDN-2 and existing stabilization methods. The results show that controlling recurrent state amplification while retaining channelwise erase gating supports improved retrieval and downstream performance, alongside competitive language modeling quality. Experimental Setup 5.1.1. DATASETS In this work, we train models through 64K-context pretraining on Prolong dataset (Gao et al., 2025). We merge the 64K and 512K ProLong data, retokenize the combined corpus with the TinyLlama (Zhang et al., 2024) tokenizer, and repack it into uniform sequences of 64K tokens. The resulting training stream contains approximately 82.78B tokens and uses next-token prediction over all non-padding tokens. Recurrent states are reset at each training-sample boundary and propagate continuously across documents within each packed sequence. 5.1.2. BASELINES We compare Stable GDN-2 with four baselines under the same training protocol. GDN-2 (Hatamizadeh et al., 2026) provides the direct reference for assessing the effect of stabilization, while KDA (Team et al., 2025) represents related delta-rule model with channel-wise forgetting. D-Clip (Su, 2026) caps each decay factor at 1/At2, making the full transition non-expansive through stronger decay while preserving the original erase gate. β-Guard (Hatamizadeh, 2026) instead shrinks channel-wise deviations of the erase gate from its key-weighted mean when needed to satisfy sufficient condition for non-expansive transitions, preserving both this mean and the original decay. Both methods retain the original GDN-2 write term. In comparison, Stable GDN-2 combines symmetric erasure with decay-regulated residual writing, as described in Section 4.1. 5.1.3. EVALUATION AND IMPLEMENTATION Evaluation. Following (Hatamizadeh et al., 2026), we assess zero-shot common-sense reasoning on nine tasks: PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2020), ARC-C and ARCE (Clark et al., 2018), OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018), SocialIQA (Sap et al., 2019), BoolQ (Clark et al., 2019), and LAMBADA (Paperno et al., 2016). We use normalized accuracy for PIQA, HellaSwag, ARC-C, ARCE, and OpenBookQA, and accuracy for the remaining tasks. For language modeling, we report WikiText (Merity et al., 2016) perplexity at 8K, 16K, 32K, and 64K windows, together with LAMBADA perplexity. We evaluate long-context retrieval capabilities on 11 task types from RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024). Specifically, S1, S2, S3, and MK1 correspond to niah single 1, niah single 2, niah single 3, and niah multikey 1, respectively. The other tasks include Multi-Query (MQ), Multi-Value (MV), Common-Word Extraction (CWE), Frequent-Word Extraction (FWE), Question Answering on HotpotQA (QAH) and SQuAD (QA-S), and Variable Tracking (VT). Evaluation uses context lengths of 32K, 64K, and 128K. Implementation. We consider two distinct 20-layer architectures with different attention configurations. The first is recurrent model consisting exclusively of linear-attention layers, while the second adopts hybrid design that repeats three linear-attention layers followed by one full-attention layer five times. Full attention covers the entire causal context. Both architectures use hidden size of 2,304 and an FFN intermediate size of 6,208. Designs respond by widening the state (Qin et al., 2024), letting it grow logarithmically (Guo et al., 2026), or externalizing it (Behrouz et al., 2025). Whether state of given size propagates without numerical degradation is separate question with older roots: long-range learning is tied to products of per-step Jacobians (Bengio et al., 1994), gradients are rescaled by their norm (Pascanu et al., 2013), and transitions may be confined to unitary matrices (Arjovsky et al., 2016). In transformers the analogue targets logits rather than states, via querykey normalization (Wortsman et al., 2024) or direct bounds on how far logits may move in one step (Anson & Aitchison, 2025). Each of these constrains single transition; accumulation is left implicit, which suffices for normal transitions but not for the non-symmetric erase matrix of GDN-2. In our work, we show that non-expansive state propagation of GDN-2 can be guaranteed through symmetric erasure, preventing cumulative amplification while preserving flexible memory updates. 7. Conclusion In this work, we identify asymmetric erasure as fundamental source of recurrent state amplification in GDN-2, showing theoretically how non-normal state transitions can accumulate across tokens and lead to numerical instability. To address this issue, we propose Stable GDN-2, which combines symmetric erasure with decay-regulated residual writing to ensure non-expansive state propagation while preserving flexible memory updates and chunkwise parallel computation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method stabilizes long-context training and delivers strong long-context retrieval and downstream task performance, while maintaining competitive language modeling quality. These findings highlight the importance of controlling recurrent state dynamics and demonstrate that numerical stability can be substantially improved without sacrificing the expressive capacity of recurrent memory.

Linear Attention and Delta-rule Models Recent advances in linear attention have improved sequence modeling through more expressive gating mechanisms and recurrent state updates (Yang et al., 2024a; 2025; Team et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026; Hatamizadeh et al., 2026). The basic formulation uses kernel feature maps to summarize the prefix in recurrent state of keyvalue outer products, allowing queries to retrieve information at cost independent of context length (Katharopoulos et al., 2020). Interpreting this recurrence as fast-weight programmer (Schlag et al., 2021) motivates replacing additive writes with delta-rule updates that selectively revise existing associations (Irie et al., 2021), while chunkwise parallel algorithms make these updates practical for training at scale (Yang et al., 2024b). parallel thread governs how long the state retains its contents, through fixed exponential decay in RetNet (Sun et al., 2023), input-dependent per-channel decay in gated linear attention (Yang et al., 2024a), depth-wise gate floors and state expansion in HGRN and HGRN2 (Qin et al., 2023; 2024), and selective discretizations in the Mamba line (Gu & Dao, 2024; Dao & Gu, 2024; Lahoti et al., 2026).
